BANKING FUNDAMENTALS — INDIA Document type: Educational domain reference
Jurisdiction: India Prepared: 11 November 2026
PURPOSE AND SCOPE This document introduces common banking products,
terminology and processes. It is intended as domain material for testing
a financial question-answering system. It is not a bank’s product
disclosure, a current interest-rate schedule, or personalised financial
advice. Product conditions vary by institution, customer, date and
applicable regulation.

A bank accepts deposits, provides loans and payment
services, and performs financial intermediation. It connects
depositors who have funds with borrowers who need funds. Banks also
support remittances, cards, account services, trade finance, cash
management and digital payments. Banks must manage risks while
meeting applicable legal and regulatory obligations.

A savings deposit account is generally used
by individuals for transactions and savings. Interest,
minimum-balance conditions, charges and transaction limits depend on
the bank’s terms and applicable rules. A current account is commonly
used by businesses and entities with frequent transactions. Interest
treatment, cash services, charges and limits depend on the bank’s
terms. A fixed deposit, also called a term deposit, places money for
a defined period under agreed conditions. The maturity amount
depends on principal, rate, compounding convention and tenure.
Premature withdrawal may be subject to conditions or penalties. A
recurring deposit involves regular contributions over a chosen
period. The maturity amount depends on the instalment schedule,
tenure and applicable rate. A deposit customer should review the
official product terms, premature-closure rules, tax treatment and
deposit-insurance information before making a decision.

Principal is the original amount borrowed,
excluding interest and charges. Interest is the cost of borrowing or
return paid on a deposit, expressed as an amount or rate. Tenor or
tenure is the length of time for which a loan or deposit runs. An
EMI, or equated monthly instalment, is a periodic payment that
typically includes principal and interest for an amortising loan.
Collateral is an asset pledged or charged to support a loan. The
lender’s rights over collateral depend on the contract and
applicable law. Loan-to-value, or LTV, is the loan amount divided by
the value of the financed asset, expressed as a percentage. A credit
score is an indicator derived from credit-history information.
Lenders may use it with income, repayment capacity, existing
obligations, collateral and other underwriting factors.

For a typical amortising loan, each
scheduled payment covers interest due for the period and reduces
outstanding principal. At the beginning of a standard repayment
schedule, the interest portion may represent a larger share of the
instalment; as principal declines, the interest portion generally
declines too, assuming the rate and schedule remain unchanged. A
floating-rate reset, missed payment, prepayment or restructuring can
change the schedule. A borrower should consult the lender’s
repayment statement for the actual outstanding balance and
instalment details.

Asset quality describes the
health of a lender’s loan portfolio. A non-performing asset, or NPA,
is a loan or advance classified as non-performing under the
applicable prudential rules. NPA classification, income recognition
and provisioning must follow the current directions applicable to
the regulated entity and facility. Do not assume one classification
rule applies to every product or institution. An NPA ratio is a
portfolio-level indicator and should be interpreted with its
definition, reporting date and context.

A lending rate may be fixed or floating. A fixed rate
is intended to remain unchanged for the agreed period, subject to
contract terms. A floating rate can change according to its
benchmark, spread and reset terms. A rate change can affect the
instalment amount, loan tenure, or both, depending on the contract
and lender policy. A model must not invent a current policy rate,
deposit rate or lending rate.

Payment systems allow money
to move between people, businesses and institutions. In India,
digital payment methods include systems such as UPI, NEFT, RTGS and
IMPS, each with its own operating rules and participant
arrangements. Customers should verify beneficiary details, protect
credentials, use official bank channels and report suspected
unauthorised transactions promptly. A bank will have defined
complaint and escalation channels; customers should consult the
current official process.

section: 8. HOW TO ANSWER BANKING QUESTIONS RELIABLY
text:
First identify the product,
institution, customer type, jurisdiction and date relevant to the
question. Distinguish a general definition from a product-specific
condition. If a question asks for an exact rate, fee, eligibility
rule, overdue threshold or regulatory requirement, consult the
latest official bank disclosure or applicable RBI direction. State
the source and effective date. If the evidence is unavailable, say
that the answer cannot be verified rather than guessing.
OFFICIAL REFERENCE POINTS Reserve Bank of India: https://www.rbi.org.in/
RBI Master Directions:
https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_ViewMasDirections.aspx RBI banking
glossary: https://shabdavali.rbi.org.in/
This educational summary does not replace official regulatory text,
contractual terms or professional financial advice.

RBI REGULATORY KNOWLEDGE — BANKING ASSET QUALITY Document type:
Educational summary with official-source references Jurisdiction: India
Prepared: 11 November 2026
PURPOSE AND SCOPE This document introduces the role of the Reserve Bank
of India and several prudential banking concepts. It is intended for
domain-specific AI testing. It is not a complete statement of law or
regulation. Regulatory requirements can change and may differ across
banks, cooperative banks, non-banking financial companies and other
regulated entities.

section: 1. ROLE OF THE RESERVE BANK OF INDIA
text:
The Reserve Bank of India, or RBI,
is India’s central bank. It performs monetary, regulatory and
supervisory functions in the financial system. Its responsibilities
include monetary policy, currency management, regulation and
supervision of specified financial institutions, payment-system
oversight and financial-stability work. Banking entities must follow
the laws, regulations, directions and circulars applicable to their
entity type and activities.

Prudential rules are intended to promote the
safety and soundness of regulated financial institutions. They
address areas such as governance, capital, liquidity, credit
exposure, asset classification, income recognition, provisioning,
disclosures and risk management. The exact requirements depend on
the regulated entity and the current applicable instrument. A
requirement for one class of institution should not automatically be
applied to another.

Income recognition rules govern when an
institution may recognise income, including interest on advances.
Recognition may depend on the status and classification of an
account and the applicable prudential framework. Accounting
recognition and cash actually received are not always the same
thing. A reliable answer should identify the relevant rule and
account category rather than assuming that every accrued amount is
automatically recognised as income.

Asset classification categorises advances
according to the applicable prudential criteria and the repayment or
credit status of the account. Categories and conditions are defined
by the relevant regulatory directions. Classification can depend on
the nature of the facility, account conduct, restructuring status
and other specified facts. The current entity-specific rule must be
checked before stating an exact overdue period or classification
threshold.

A non-performing asset, or NPA, is an advance
classified as non-performing under the applicable RBI prudential
framework. Classification depends on the relevant directions, the
nature of the facility and the facts of the account. A model must
not give a universal overdue-day threshold without checking the
applicable current rule and any relevant exceptions. If a user asks
whether a particular loan is an NPA, the answer may require
account-level facts that are not available in a general document.

Provisioning recognises that some loan exposures may
not be fully recovered. It affects reported profitability and the
carrying value of assets. Provisioning requirements can vary by
asset category, security, borrower, restructuring status and the
applicable regulatory framework. A provision is not necessarily the
same as a final write-off. A write-off is an accounting action and
does not by itself mean that the borrower’s obligation has been
legally extinguished.

Gross NPA and net NPA
measures are commonly used to describe aspects of a bank’s stressed
advances. Their definitions and calculation details should be taken
from the relevant reporting framework. A ratio should always be
accompanied by its reporting date, denominator and source.
Comparisons between institutions may be misleading if definitions,
portfolios, reporting periods or accounting treatment differ. A
single ratio does not explain the full credit-risk position.

Regulatory information changes. Before
relying on a threshold, effective date, exemption or reporting
requirement:
- Identify the regulated entity type, such as a commercial bank, small
finance bank, cooperative bank or NBFC.
- Find the latest RBI direction or circular for that entity and topic.
- Check the effective date, amendments and transitional provisions.
- Identify the exact chapter, paragraph or section supporting the
claim.
- Distinguish binding regulatory text from explanatory articles or
commentary.
- If the source is unavailable or ambiguous, state the limitation
rather than guessing.

Question: What overdue period makes a loan
an NPA? A safe answer is: The applicable classification criteria
depend on the type of regulated entity and facility and the current
RBI directions. I would need to identify the institution and
facility type and verify the latest applicable direction before
giving an exact threshold. This avoids presenting a rule for one
category as if it applied to all lenders.

Master Directions portal:
https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_ViewMasDirections.aspx RBI
Financial Stability Report portal:
https://www.rbi.org.in/scripts/FSReports.aspx RBI official website:
https://www.rbi.org.in/
Always select the correct entity-specific direction and check
amendments. This educational summary is not legal, regulatory or
financial advice and does not reproduce the full official text.

section: FINANCIAL RISK MANAGEMENT — CONCEPTS FOR DOMAIN QUESTION ANSWERING
text:
Document type: Educational domain reference Scope: Banking and
financial-system risk concepts Prepared: 11 November 2026
PURPOSE AND SCOPE This document describes common financial risks and
principles for evaluating AI answers in a banking context. It is
intended as educational domain material and a starting point for model
testing. It does not provide investment recommendations, credit
decisions or institution-specific regulatory limits.

Credit risk is the possibility that a borrower or
counterparty will fail to meet contractual obligations. Common
assessment factors include repayment history, income and cash-flow
capacity, leverage, collateral, industry conditions and
concentration. Credit risk can arise from loans, bonds, derivatives,
settlement exposures and other counterparty relationships. A credit
decision should not be based on one indicator alone. A credit score
may be useful, but it does not replace affordability analysis,
verification and applicable underwriting policy.

Liquidity risk is the risk that an institution cannot
meet cash-flow obligations when due without unacceptable losses. A
bank may be solvent but still face liquidity pressure if it cannot
obtain cash quickly enough to meet withdrawals or payments. Banks
manage liquidity through cash and liquid-asset buffers, funding
diversification, maturity monitoring, contingency funding plans and
stress testing. Liquidity risk should be assessed across different
time horizons and under both normal and stressed conditions.

Market risk is the possibility of loss from movements in
market prices or rates, including interest rates, foreign exchange
rates, equity prices and commodity prices. Exposure depends on
positions, sensitivities, hedges and market conditions. A change in
market rates can affect the value of assets and liabilities
differently. A risk report should state the relevant portfolio,
valuation date, assumptions and measurement method.

Operational risk arises from inadequate or failed
processes, people, systems or external events. Examples include
processing errors, cyber incidents, fraud, third-party failures,
internal misconduct and business disruption. Controls include
segregation of duties, access management, reconciliation, staff
training, incident response, audit trails and business continuity
planning. Controls reduce exposure but cannot guarantee that
incidents will never occur.

Concentration risk occurs when exposures are
heavily concentrated in a borrower, connected group, sector,
geography, funding source or asset class. A concentrated portfolio
can be vulnerable to a common adverse event. Diversification and
exposure limits can reduce, but do not eliminate, this risk.
Concentration should be examined by relevant dimensions and with
clear definitions of exposure.

Capital provides a loss-absorbing buffer. Capital
adequacy frameworks compare eligible capital with risk-weighted
exposures or other prescribed measures. Capital definitions,
deductions, buffers and minimum ratios are regulatory matters and
must be checked against the current rule applicable to the
institution. A model should not quote an exact regulatory capital
minimum without identifying the entity type, applicable framework
and effective date.

Stress testing evaluates how a portfolio or
institution might perform under severe but plausible adverse
scenarios. Scenarios may include recession, rising defaults, falling
asset prices, interest-rate shocks, deposit outflows or
foreign-exchange movements. Results depend on assumptions, data
quality, model design and management actions. Stress-test results
are not forecasts and should not be presented as predictions of what
will certainly happen. Sensitivity analysis can help show which
assumptions have the largest effect.

Effective risk governance includes clear
accountability, independent oversight, documented policies, reliable
data, escalation processes and regular review. Risk limits should
have owners and procedures for handling breaches. Senior management
and boards need information that is timely, accurate and
understandable. A model-generated risk summary should preserve
uncertainty and should not replace accountable human review.

Model risk is the possibility that
decisions or outcomes are adversely affected by errors in model
design, assumptions, data, implementation or use. A financial-domain
AI system can introduce additional risks if it invents facts,
misquotes a regulation, confuses products or presents uncertain
output as certain. Reliability work should test representative
questions, edge cases, ambiguous wording, outdated information and
questions that cannot be answered from the supplied documents.

- Separate sourced facts from calculations, assumptions and opinions.
- Cite the document, section and date supporting material claims.
- Do not invent regulatory thresholds, rates, financial results or
citations.
- State when information is missing, outdated or conflicting.
- Ask for the institution type, product, jurisdiction and as-of date
when these affect the answer.
- For numerical calculations, show inputs, formula, units and
rounding.
- Avoid presenting general information as personalised investment,
lending or legal advice.
- Escalate high-impact or customer-specific decisions to qualified
human review.
